title: Calder: Andrew's actual household
standfirst: Andrew’s testament names Elizat and their son Robert. The Duddingston Robert is now the preferred uncertain adult continuation, with the earlier burgh-parent pair retained as alternatives.
question: Who were Andrew's parents, and where did his named children and land pass next?
answer: Andrew's testament names wife Elizat Stevinsoun, son Robert and daughters Marion, Janet and Isobel. It names no son James, and it names no parent. Robert has a checked existing profile and a preferred uncertain Duddingston continuation; the other children’s later identities remain under review; a chronologically possible John of Glasgow is not a documented father.

chapters.title: Duddingston’s Robert: the Corsoun household as preferred uncertain parents
body: The preferred local working parents of the Duddingston Robert are now Andrew Glasgow and Elizat Stevinsoun, through possible identity with their recorded son Robert-4006. The accepted 1597/8 testament expressly names Robert as Andrew’s son by Elizat and makes provision until he reached age. A minor then can fit the adult generation of the Robert buried at Duddingston in 1647 and the probable father of James the Edinburgh weaver. The retained circa-1582 and 1597/before-1597 dates are estimates or bounds, not two exact birth records in conflict. On the maintained, queried Calder-area reading of Andrew’s residence, this offers a positive named-child family candidate in the relevant broad Lothian comparison. The earlier Archibald/Isobell pair has no record naming the Duddingston Robert as its child. Prefer the recorded Corsoun family as the uncertain route, with both former parents retained as alternatives.

The 1598 child and the Duddingston adult remain separate WikiTree profiles with an uncertain identity comparison; no merge is inferred. No holding, occupation, wife or named-relative bridge equates them, and the Corsoun/Calder place reading itself remains queried. A different local Robert, including the separate Ninian-son account Robert-1027, remains a comparison. Ninian’s son keeps his proved parents and is not conflated with Andrew’s named son. Elizat’s maternity is direct for the recorded child only; it is uncertain for the Duddingston adult because it depends on the same identity hypothesis. Archibald’s and Isobell’s biological parentage is not disproved. James-1150’s probable father assessment, all other selected families, and the adult’s existing vital fields remain unchanged. Two modern Robert accounts can represent one historical son; they are not independent evidence for two sons.

One paternal and one maternal working choice are replaced, affecting a child side of 64 pre-1850 profiles. This improves the source basis of the preferred route, without raising either adult parent link above uncertain. Existing live parent fields and flags remain unchanged. The record-son’s already-confident father is reaffirmed, while Elizat’s recorded motherhood and the Andrew–Elizat spouse relationship receive formal documented assessments. The main view also reconciles already-completed profile redirects and the previously corrected public 1598 household; these are publication repairs, not new historical people or newly discovered records.

chapters.period: 1687–1755 · two uncertain fathers and one uncertain mother
chapters.title: Calder and Irvine: selected uncertain parent families
body: Select William Glasgow-1026 as the uncertain working father of John Glasgow-3481, the combined Calder father account recorded in 1730 and with Christian Meek in 1751–1755. This adopts possible identity with John Glasgow-1544, the child indexed at Kirknewton in 1702 with father William. The same name and parish and a normal adult generation favour this concrete child account over an unidentified origin: if baptised near birth in 1702, he would be about 28 in 1730 and 53 at the 1755 child. Those ages are conditional examples, not ages stated in the registers. The old circa 1710 birth was inferred from assumed age at the 1730 fatherhood and cannot exclude the 1702 child. The child’s existing father identity as William-1026 is itself qualified; no record explicitly identifies the later Meek husband as his son.

John-1544 and John-3481 remain separate profile accounts of a possible single man; the selection does not establish two distinct John sons. The 1702 date remains unreconciled: the child’s field uses a before 11 November boundary while its biography cites a 29 November baptism. Neither date is newly corrected. The later account combines the 1730 father of Jean, whose mother is omitted, with the 1751 and 1755 Meek household. That earlier adult identification remains a preferred working combination, not a continuous household proved by occupation, land or witnesses. John-81, estimated born 1709, remains a specific competing identity for the 1730 father. His Guthrie household is indexed with children in West Calder in 1751 and 1753 while the Meek household appears in Kirknewton in 1751 and Leith in 1755. That concrete overlap makes a simple succession of wives less persuasive; do not combine the full Guthrie and Meek families without resolving the entries. No birth estimate alone excludes John-81. Other local John origins remain possible. Ann McCook is not selected as John-3481’s mother: the reviewed 1702 child citation names William, and the attached Ann field does not supply an independently verified maternal clause. William’s existing uncertain John-3610 father and older family alternatives retain their grades; no date or family field is changed to force the new route.

Select John Glasgow-1057 and Agnes Spark-330 as the uncertain working parents of George Glasgow-4165, father with Margt at Irvine in 1741–1745. The preferred model uses possible identity with their son George Glasgow-1058, baptised at Kilwinning on 20 November 1687 and already associated with the George/Margaret Martain couple indexed marrying there on 11 June 1728. That couple’s son George-3312 is indexed at Kilwinning in 1729. The nearby Irvine household later repeats George and Margt, with no maternal surname or father’s age stated. This offers a specific existing couple and a compatible continuation across neighbouring parishes. On an infant-baptism assumption, the elder George would be about 54–58 at the Irvine children; late fatherhood remains possible. Margaret’s circa 1704 estimate would fit an adult mother in 1741–1745, but it is only a marriage-derived estimate. Neither calculation proves the identities or a move.

Agnes Spark’s proposed maternity is assessed independently from the same positive child evidence: the 1687 baptism index explicitly names John Glasgow and Agnes Spark as George’s parents. Their already confident parentage for the recorded child is not newly upgraded. Transferring either parent to the Irvine adult depends on the uncertain child/groom/Irvine identity chain, so both new adult links remain uncertain. They share that premise and are correlated, not independent confirmations. Margt in the 1741–1745 entries is George’s co-parent, not evidence for his own mother; Margaret Martin is not assigned a new mother or merged with any other Margaret.

The 1687 child, 1728 groom and Irvine father may be different men. The match of Margt to Margaret Martin is compatible, not a full recorded maternal surname match, and no age, occupation or property bridges the two parishes. The existing 1687-child/1728-adult family account also needs its identity assessment kept separate from the child’s explicit parent clause. A younger George from the Irvine Hugh/Service, James/Rae or another local family remains possible. The proposed father James-4158 would give a normal generation if George was born around 1720, but no record names him as George’s father; the specific older George/Margaret household is preferred provisionally. Keep the merchant son George-3312 distinct. If his 1729 entry represents infant baptism, he would be only about 12 at the 1741 fatherhood, a strong objection to assigning those children directly to that son. The index event type and adult-child identities still require their own review; an unsupported older birth estimate must not decide them. No merchant trade, Nethermains ownership, Manchester patent or artillery career is transferred to the Irvine father. No identity merge, duplicate removal or live relationship save is performed.

Two selected uncertain fathers and one separately assessed uncertain mother using existing parish and profile research. No new original inspection, certainty upgrade, identity merge or live WikiTree save. John’s new mother remains unknown. Existing dates, recorded couples, earlier uncertain routes and possible duplicate accounts are retained; connectivity measures profile accounts, not proved distinct individuals.

chapters.title: Dublin watchmakers and Irvine: two uncertain fathers
body: Select Thomas Glasgow-1242 as the uncertain working father of Philip Glasco-146. The preferred model uses Glasco-146 as the elder Dublin watchmaker account, retaining the 1711 Scottish child Glasgow-1241 as a separate possible account of the same man. That child’s Uphall index names father Thomas; his existing research already retains the elder watchmaker as a compatible adult identity. The Glasco-146 account has the Christ Church Lane watchmaking association in 1752, an estimated birth about 1715 and a younger Philip in its tree family, which suit that provisional elder role. The four-year difference from the 1711 baptism is between a record and an unsupported estimate, not a concrete identity conflict. This materialises the existing Scottish candidate at low confidence; it does not prove migration or two distinct elder Philips.

The Dublin records name no Scottish parents, birthplace or apprenticeship, so the Scottish child and elder watchmaker may be different men. The fresh Glasco-146 biography itself mixes the 1752 watchmaker with junior notices of 1765,1768 and 1770. Its c.1715 birth and the c.1740 birth of Glasco-147 are tree estimates, not evidence selecting a generation. If Glasco-146 instead represents the junior, the elder Philip is an alternative father-generation placement and the Thomas link would need revision; no competing father is attached alongside it. The elder placement is a preferred working interpretation of the profile’s trade/address and family structure, not a claim that every event in that biography belongs to him. The junior’s 1765 unnamed-wife death,1768 Teresa Plunkett marriage and reported 1770 death remain with the younger documentary account Glasgow-3932. Glasco-147 is a strongly supported duplicate account of that younger man, but its quoted 1772 younger/inventory wording was not independently rechecked here and establishes neither the estimated birth nor a newly verified father clause; a grant date is not a death date. No merge, spouse transfer or new child attachment follows. Catherine Mangan is called Glasco-146’s mother in its prose but spouse in its structured family; the 1750 report describes the elder’s bride only as the widow Mangan, and the 1760 report gives no forename. Neither record proves maternity. Preserve the existing Mangan/Braccan and younger-parent fields as qualified leads; do not add a mother for Glasco-146. The father Thomas is common to the retained 1711 child records, while the 3 June Uphall versus 21 October Linlithgow Philip entries and their maternal readings remain unreconciled; Jean Duncan is not transferred as Glasco-146’s mother. The 1777 probate/court occurrence does not establish survival after 1772. The local elder account uses 1772 as an uncertain death year through the selected identity, retaining the old after 1772 value and all junior events in the comparison.

Select Hugh Glasgow-3109, father with Jean Service at Irvine in 1696, as the very low-confidence working father of James Glasgow-4158, father with Margaret/Marion Rae at Irvine in 1721–1723. This extends an actual local household across a compatible generation. A James born in the later 1690s could be a son of the 1696 household and an adult father by 1721; this is a compatibility example, not a new birth estimate. Hugh’s proposed identity with the 1676 Kilwinning child would make him a young father in the 1690s, which fits that example. The shared uncommon surname, same parish and two successive family generations favour this existing named parent model; no register entry names James’s father.

James could instead be a son of the Irvine John-2475/Isabell Kyle family, Michael-1406’s household, another Ayrshire family, or an unrecorded father. The named James child of John/Isabell indexed in 1711 would be only about ten at the 1721 fatherhood if baptised as an infant, so he is a weaker identity candidate unless an older-baptism explanation is established. James’s before 1702 boundary is an adult-status estimate, not an actual birth. If James were substantially older, Hugh’s proposed 1676 child identity would become less plausible; no date is changed to make either hypothesis fit. The older Hugh/Hew account, its existing uncertain parents, Jean Service/Mary Dean identity sequence and earlier alternatives remain as previously assessed. James’s merged Margaret/Marion Rae household remains a working combined father account; no remarriage or equivalence between the mothers is proved. The 1740 Prosperity of Irvine shipmaster is still a possible occupational identity only, with no transfer of occupation, voyage or trade to this father. Jean Service is not selected as James’s mother solely from Hugh’s co-parentage.

Two newly selected uncertain fathers, no new mother, identity merge, certainty upgrade or live WikiTree save. Existing newspaper/parish reviews supply the historical comparisons; three Open/non-living WikiTree profiles were read anonymously to reconcile their current wording. The elder’s 1772 death is conditional on the selected adult identity; no birth is changed. Possible duplicate profile accounts and inherited uncertain routes remain explicit limitations of the working connectivity score.

The anonymous Open-profile capture of Glasgow-3932 on 16 October 2026 contains Robert Glasgow’s Kilrea 1827 biography, not the Dublin watchmaker. The entire misplaced text is also preserved in the captured biography of the correct Robert Glasgow-3897. A complete sourced Dublin replacement is prepared locally; the real current biography remains available in the comparison, with its hash retained. No Robert birth, relatives or life events are transferred to Philip. The structured Dublin profile and the current Glasco-147/Teresa Plunkett family support retaining the earlier strong same-person match between the two younger-Philip profiles, without a live merge or duplicate spouse attachment.

chapters.period: 1648–1735 · two uncertain fathers and one uncertain mother
chapters.title: Libberton and Uphall: selected uncertain parent families
body: Select Johne Glasgow-3093, indexed at Mid Calder in 1648 as son of Jamis Glasgow, as the very low-confidence working father of Robert Glasgow-4168, father at Libberton in 1718–1726. The preferred local route runs through Johne’s existing uncertain James-3332 father identity and that James’s possible identification with the Lindsaylands weaver indexed in 1680. Lindsaylands and Quothquan/Libberton supply the adjacent Lanarkshire family setting; Mid Calder is a separate parish and no migration is proved. A Johne born around 1648 could father Robert in the 1680s–1690s, allowing ordinary adult fatherhood at the 1718 baptism. This generation is preferred over assigning Robert directly to the older weaver, who was dead by 1680 if that identity is correct. It is a specific family hypothesis using recorded men, not a father clause in Robert’s records.

Johne’s only reviewed record is the 1648 child entry; no later occupation, residence, spouse or death identifies him with Libberton. The Jamis-to-Glasgow-3332 identity and the latter’s Lindsaylands identity are both uncertain. Its inherited circa 1634 birth would make him only about fourteen at Johne’s 1648 event if literal; that unsourced estimate must not establish or exclude parentage. The 1648 source names Jamis, not John-1084. The known parish association therefore belongs to a conditional family chain, not to an independently followed migration. James-3332 himself remains an alternative father if Robert was born before 1680 and fathered the later children at an older age. The son James apprenticed in Edinburgh in 1690, explicitly son of deceased James the Lindsaylands weaver, is a genuine alternative intermediate father or uncle; his existing held draft is retained, and no unrecorded generation is invented. The 1624 Quothquan weaver is a separate death account; its early death makes direct paternity of a 1718–1726 father much less plausible. Robert’s merged Gibson/Watson household remains a working combined account, not proof of remarriage or identity between the two women. No mother is selected for Robert, and no vital date is changed to fit the route.

Select John Glasgow-1105 and Agnes Eastone-3 as the uncertain working parents of Thomas Glasgow-1226, the father with Catherine Clarkson/Classon at Uphall from 1717 and Livingston by 1730. This selects possible identity with their named Linlithgow child Thomas Glasgow-1242 of 1675, while retaining both profile accounts. That child would be about 42 at the 1717 Margaret entry and about 60 at the 1735 Hellen entry: later fatherhood, but chronologically possible. The existing Glasgow-1242 account also represents a Thomas/Jean Duncan household at Uphall in 1704. Recurring Thomas name, the same Uphall parish and a plausible succession of households provide a more specific route than the removed Kilbirnie-minister parents. The 1675 parent clause belongs directly to the child account; transferring it to the Clarkson adult depends wholly on the uncertain identity.

Agnes’s maternity is assessed separately: the 1675 FamilySearch parent index explicitly identifies Agnes Eastone in Thomas Glesgow’s entry, while John is named as father in the paired child citation. This is a positive maternal source for that child, not merely John’s spouse field. Agnes’s attachment to the Clarkson adult remains uncertain because the child/adult identity is uncertain. Eastone/Daston readings, her estimated birth and John’s own child/adult identification remain qualified. These two new parent links share one identity premise and are correlated, not independent confirmations of the adult’s ancestry.

The 1675 child, the Duncan adult and the Clarkson adult may represent one, two or three men. There is no inspected age, occupation, marriage, widowhood or probate bridge. The 1701 Duncan marriage is reported family information, not a newly inspected register. No death of Jean, remarriage to Catherine or overlap resolution is invented. The differing Philip 1711 dates in the Thomas research compilation and the Glasgow-1242 biography, and the omission of a mother in the latter’s indexed child, do not establish a continuous Duncan household or certain maternity. They are not two independent confirmations. Catherine’s indexed surname variants remain as recorded. The before 1700 boundary for the Clarkson adult and the 2/21 February 1675 date discrepancy in the child account remain unchanged. The 1666 St Cuthbert’s Thomas-1311, child of Alexander and Issobell Anderson, remains a compatible identity alternative, albeit with fatherhood at about 51–69 in 1717–1735. His possible identification with the Edinburgh writer whose testament was indexed in 1691 is unproved and cannot be used to exclude him. The retained 1766 grave link is an unverified namesake comparison, not an established death for the Clarkson adult. The 1663 Thomas-3091 and an otherwise unrecorded local Thomas also remain possible. No identity merge or live attachment is performed.

Two selected uncertain fathers and one separately assessed uncertain mother, using existing parish, testament and apprenticeship reviews. No new original inspection, certainty upgrade, identity merge, spouse change or vital-date alteration. Robert’s new mother remains unknown. The Thomas parent pair depends on possible child/adult identity; profile-based connectivity retains potentially duplicate accounts and is not a count of proved distinct ancestors.

chapters.title: Quothquan and Thankerton: two uncertain fathers
body: Select Stephen Glasgow-1029 as the uncertain working father of James Glasgow-3910. James’s weaver occupation and Quothquan locality favour using the 1612 court defender and the 1624 testator as one working adult account. Stephen is documented as an adult in Glasgow in 1575 and with wife Margaret Grahame in 1582; his approximate 1550 birth is an estimate, not a birth record. The existing tree already places John Glasgow-3296, the 1650 Quothquan testator, under Stephen, uncertain. The preferred model treats the two early Quothquan men as paternal brothers rather than making the later John James’s father. A Stephen born around the mid-sixteenth century could have fathered James in the 1570s–1590s and John in a similar generation. This uses a named family already connected to Quothquan, at very low confidence, rather than inventing a missing parent. No record names Stephen as James’s father or James and John as brothers.

The route depends both on the proposed James–John brotherhood and on John’s already uncertain Stephen parentage. The Glasgow–Montfoid–Mid Calder–Quothquan identities are not proved migrations. John’s 1650 testament names his sister Bessie and no child or parent; omission of James, already dead by 1624, does not disprove brotherhood. John himself could instead be James’s father if older than his inherited estimate, or the men could be uncle/nephew, cousins or unrelated local namesakes. The older John and Thomas tenants in the 1520s–1530s remain possible ancestral relatives with unproved intervening generations; no direct father edge to them is selected. Margaret Grahame is Stephen’s documented spouse in 1582, not a documented mother of James, so no mother is attached. John’s existing mother field and all earlier parent and identity alternatives remain unchanged.

Select the Quothquan weaver James Glasgow-3910 as the uncertain working father of Helen Glasgow-3909, the married Thankerton woman whose testament was indexed in January 1627. The shared uncommon surname, neighbouring Quothquan/Thankerton locality and an adult weaver recorded at the 1612 hearing followed by a married woman dead by 1627 give a coherent father/daughter generation. Helen’s circa-1605 birth is an inherited estimate, not her stated age; it is compatible with a James born before the mid-1590s but is not independent proof of that generation. This is a low-confidence local family selection. No inspected record calls Helen James’s daughter.

Helen could instead be James’s sister or niece, a daughter of the later John or another local Glasgow. Neither testament index supplies her age, children or parents. Thankerton is her household’s stated residence, not a proved birthplace or death place. Margaret Threipland’s 1626 Quothquan widow entry remains a possible wife for James, not a selected spouse identity and not a mother for Helen. Both newly considered mothers remain unknown. The original 1624 and 1627 testaments are discriminating follow-up evidence, not a prerequisite for displaying these qualified working links.

The circa-1605 birth estimate is replaced locally by an explicitly conditional adult-role estimate, before 1595: this assumes an age of at least 18 at the 1612 hearing and the preferred same-weaver identification. Neither the record nor the profile supplies a real age, so this is not a recorded birthday or a hard biological exclusion. The 1607–1608 acts concern the earlier dispute, not a newly established birth or exact adult-age observation. The 26 July 1624 date is a testament confirmation, so death is shown as before that date and its place is left unresolved; Quothquan is the stated residence. Imported profile values remain in the comparison and the earlier biography is retained as history.

Two selected uncertain local fathers; no new mother, original-source inspection, live WikiTree edit, identity merge or certainty upgrade. The family placements use existing record reviews, named local accounts and checked chronology; paternal/full sibling status remains conditional. The circa-1605 birth estimate is replaced locally by an explicitly conditional adult-role estimate, before 1595: this assumes an age of at least 18 at the 1612 hearing and the preferred same-weaver identification. Neither the record nor the profile supplies a real age, so this is not a recorded birthday or a hard biological exclusion. The 1607–1608 acts concern the earlier dispute, not a newly established birth or exact adult-age observation. The 26 July 1624 date is a testament confirmation, so death is shown as before that date and its place is left unresolved; Quothquan is the stated residence. Imported profile values remain in the comparison and the earlier biography is retained as history.

James Glasgow-3332 remains a surviving cross-profile identity alternative for the 1624 Quothquan weaver. Its circa-1634 birth is an unsupported estimate and cannot by itself exclude that earlier man. Identification with the distinct weaver indexed at Back of Lindsaylands in 1680 would exclude a death before 1624 if established, but that later identity is itself only possible. Retain Glasgow-3910 as the record-defined 1624 account for the selected uncertain family; do not merge the profiles or transfer Glasgow-3332’s unproved parent and child attachments. Those existing family fields remain unchanged, and the proposed Stephen placement is an alternative to that account’s current pedigree.

chapters.title: Michael of Irvine and James of Kirknewton: two working fathers
body: Select Robert Glasgow-1512 as Michael Glasgow-1406’s uncertain working father. This activates a parent comparison already recorded in Michael’s profile. Robert is a record-defined Ayr father with Margaret Donald in 1670 and 1671; Michael is recorded as an Irvine skinner in 1679 and is already treated locally as the later saddler/councillor. Robert’s before 1652 birth is an upper-bound estimate from his later children, not evidence that he was born in 1652. Michael’s before 1679 boundary likewise does not date his birth. An older Robert and a Michael born well before the summons could fit a father/son generation; their ages are not recorded. The regional family setting and existing candidate justify a very low-confidence working choice. No record names Michael’s father, and no shared occupation, holding, witness or household identifies this Robert as his parent.

John Glasgow-1604 is another viable older father generation, rather than a disproved alternative. Robert’s own attachment to that John is unproved, and taking John’s approximate 1626 date narrowly could press the generation spacing if Robert had Michael early. Those older dates and attachments remain hypotheses; no date is adjusted to repair the pedigree. Another Ayrshire father, or a sibling/collateral relationship to Robert, remains possible. Margaret Donald-1722 is named in Robert’s 1670–1671 children’s records, not in a record naming Michael’s mother. She is not selected as Michael’s mother. The existing 1679 skinner/later saddler/councillor identification is inherited from the completed merge, not newly proved; keep the 1679 summons,1686/1702 civic records and 1699/1701 leather-work references distinct in their evidence roles. Elizabeth Garven and Catharine Baird remain the recorded mothers in Michael’s later child group. The 1700 Elizabeth entry has an assumed year and no proved 1 January birthday. No mother, marriage or death date is newly inferred for Michael, and the 1700–1715 household chronology does not itself identify his parents. The earlier proof-level hold on Robert is retained as history, not treated as a disproof of this qualified local model.

Select the older William Glasgow-1026 as James Glasgow-3526’s uncertain working father. William’s Kirknewton household is documented by Bessie in 1682 and William in 1705. James is the father-name account behind John’s 1717 Kirknewton/East Calder entry, with a Helen 1714 association held in a collaborative tree. James’s 1688 birth is an unsupported profile estimate. If the rough 1660/1688 generations are close, William would have been about 28 at his birth, and the proposed son falls between William’s already recorded children. This same-area, compatible household generation is preferred provisionally, at low confidence. The combined Kirknewton/East Calder label does not establish the exact historic parish or continuous residence, and no record names William as James’s father.

John-3525’s earlier biography links its father to James Glasgow-1547, whereas the maintained local family uses James-3526. The 1717 index names James, not either modern profile ID. James-1547, associated with Andrew Glasgow-1546 and a 1702 entry, remains a surviving alternative childhood identity for the adult father. If baptised as an infant in 1702 he would be about 15 in 1717 and about 12 at Helen’s tree-held 1714 date. That makes the ordinary older-William model more straightforward, but neither a later childhood baptism nor an erroneous Helen association is excluded. No merge or categorical biological exclusion is selected. Andrew-1546 therefore remains an alternative father through that identity, not a newly attached parent. Andrew-1319 or another older Calder father remains possible. William-3974, the separate 1671 child of Andro, would imply younger fatherhood at a literal 1688 birth; the date estimates alone do not exclude him. Do not undo the split between that child and the older William-1026. The already attached Irish James-1025 may be another account of this James, a relative or an unrelated namesake. Sharing a proposed father does not prove two distinct James sons, and no Scottish-to-Tyrone identity or migration is established. Ann McCook is not selected as James’s mother, and Christian Cook’s attachment to James-1547 is not transferred. James’s wife and the two children’s mothers remain unknown. Helen’s exact 1714 date and father association are tree-held, not an inspected baptism. John’s 1717 record supplies a father name but not a birth or parents for the adult James. The existing child-parent grades, James’s estimated 1688 field, William’s selected uncertain John-3610 father and all older alternatives are preserved.

Both are selected uncertain local father models using existing material. Neither adult receives a mother. No original newly inspected, source-record discovery, identity merge, live WikiTree edit or confidence upgrade is claimed. Existing dates, places and attached relatives are retained; connectivity counts profile accounts, including possible duplicates and older uncertain links.

chapters.title: Two Lothian family heads: the Duffe and Kirknewton households
body: Select Johnne Glasgow-1151 as the uncertain working father of James Glasgow-2682, husband of Isobell Duffe. James’s captured biography already proposes Johnne as a possible father. The Inveresk and Musselburgh index records Johnne on25 November 1632 with father Alexander Glasgow. James and Isobell’s Edinburgh children begin with Jean on13 April 1677. If Johnne was baptised near birth and James’s approximate 1655 birth is close, Johnne would have been about 23 at James’s birth and 44 at the first known grandchild’s baptism. This is an ordinary father/son generation within the wider Lothian setting. Select that already recorded comparison provisionally, at very low confidence. Neither James’s own birth nor Johnne’s adult life is established; this is a parent-generation model, not a source naming James’s father.

James Glasgow-3076, recorded at St Cuthbert’s in 1661 with father James Glasgow-3077 and mother Annapill Glessie, remains an alternative childhood identity explicitly suggested in that child’s profile. If baptised as an infant he would have been about 16 at Jean’s 1677 baptism; that younger parenthood makes it less straightforward than the selected ordinary-generation model, but does not exclude him. An older-child baptism also remains possible. John Glasgow-1084 is another previously proposed father. His Gordon/Berwickshire household and separate James Glasgow-3107 account remain viable comparisons; no missing death or marriage is treated as an exclusion. A different unrecorded father remains possible, and the shortlist is not exhaustive. No source joins Johnne’s 1632 child record to an adult father of James, supplies James’s age, or connects their households by craft, witness, property or inheritance. The preference is weak, based on the existing candidate, chronology and regional fit; the component gain supplies no identity evidence. No mother is selected for James. Johnne’s index names Alexander but no mother; his existing Clerk attachment does not establish a mother for James. Keep the Duffe household distinct from the Edinburgh weaver Glasgow-1150 and the unresolved Whitecastle James Glasgow-1376. The old 1657 event on1376 names James as father of Marione, not as the child. That role error does not supply a birth or parentage for the Duffe husband. The old reference to “James-1168,about1540” also mislabels the Corsankell elder; the selected route instead uses Johnne’s actual recorded father Alexander Glasgow-1148. The 1679 and 1680 sons called James remain separate child accounts; no infant death or survivor marrying Jean Dobie is newly established. The 1679 mother’s indexed Elizabeth/Isobell Duffe difference remains an existing household-identity qualification. All six children, spouse, dates and previous assessments are preserved.

Select John Glasgow-3610 as the uncertain working father of William Glasgow-1026, the older Kirknewton householder associated with Ann McCook by 1682. This activates the same-parish candidate already retained in William’s research. A 1649 Kirknewton/East Calder index names Johne Glasgow as the father of the child Johne; the adult account also carries a Margaret comparison with unresolved 1646/1649 dates. A father active in 1649 could have another son around William’s estimated 1660 birth. If the adult John is the 1608 Mid Calder child used in his own selected family model, he would have been about 52 in 1660, chronologically possible for a father. That childhood identity is itself uncertain and is not required for the local parent generation to remain possible. The common parish setting and compatible parent generation favour this existing John comparison over restoring the younger Walter-1554 as William’s father or importing the weak Kilwinning John-1604 comparison. Select John at low confidence. No inspected baptism, marriage, testament or property record names William as this John’s son.

William Glasgow-1026 is the older father in the 1682 household, not William Glasgow-3974, the child born/baptised in 1671 with father Andro Glasgow. Do not restore the 1671 child’s father to the older man. Walter Glasgow-1554 was indexed in 1649 and would be only about eleven at a literal 1660 birth; retain him as a non-selected former proposal, not a restored father. William’s 1660 date is an estimate, so that subtraction is not a newly proved biological exclusion. Other older Calder Glasgows, including William-1087 or Robert-4006, remain possible father-generation alternatives without a parent clause. John-1604’s Ayrshire route is retained as a weaker geographic comparison. John-3610’s own selected father John-3296 and possible identity with the 1608 John-1086 remain uncertain. The uncertain adult Alexander-3118 attachment is not a proved 1650 baptism and supplies no independent sibling evidence. No mother is selected for William. The 1649 source names only the father in this review; Ann McCook is William’s existing co-parent/spouse account, not evidence of his mother. Preserve the current wives, children and their individual evidence grades. The new father route does not validate the unsupported Captain Robert-2867 or Irish James-1025 parentage, a Tyrone migration, the legacy Tyrone death-place field, or the unsourced Walter middle name. The 1682–1705 same-father household reconstruction and the wider descendant accounts keep their existing uncertainty. A large working component is not a proved pedigree. No vital date, location, spouse or current attachment is cleared to force the new parent.

Both father selections are expressly uncertain local hypotheses using existing material. No new mother, original inspection, live WikiTree edit, identity merge or confidence upgrade is claimed. The fixed cohort and all confidently marked connectivity measurements must remain unchanged. Counts describe retained profile accounts and inherit uncertainty in older links, including possible duplicates.

chapters.title: Issobell: a Mid Calder childhood for the McCaskie bride
body: Select David Glasgow-1028 as the uncertain working father of Issobell Glasgow-3185, the bride indexed with Robert McCaskie at St Cuthbert’s on 19 July 1632, through possible identity with David’s Mid Calder daughter Issobell Glasgow-1085, baptised on 3 May 1612. This adopts an existing comparison in the captured child profile, rather than inventing a new named parent from the marriage alone. Exact forename and surname, the compatible Lothian setting and an age of about twenty in 1632 if baptised near birth favour this childhood as a practical working choice. The child’s baptism names David, but neither it nor the marriage supplies the bridge between child and adult. Shared name and compatible chronology do not prove the identity. Prefer this young-adult explanation provisionally over an older widow or an unrecorded childhood, at low confidence.

Retain Glasgow-1085 and Glasgow-3185 as separate profile accounts of a possible single woman; the selected parent does not establish two distinct daughters called Issobell. The father–daughter link is already confidently marked for the record-defined 1612 child; only the transfer to the 1632 bride is newly selected and uncertain. The marriage index names no father, age, birthplace, prior marital status or children. The 19 July date belongs to a combined banns/marriages index and is not newly verified as the ceremony date. The bride’s before-1612 birth boundary is an inferred profile estimate, not a birth record or an independently established exclusion of the May 1612 child. It is retained unchanged; no new birth date is entered to force the connection. The child’s 1642 Hardington, Somerset death fields remain an unsourced tree-held later-life lead in this review, not a verified fate or proof of migration. Even if correct, that later date alone would not exclude the 1632 marriage. The older Isobel Glasgow-3336, who represents Andrew’s testament-named daughter and is probably the William Symountoun bride of 1619 and mother of the 1620 child, remains a possible remarriage alternative. No death of Symountoun, remarriage record or continuing incompatible household was inspected; do not exclude her merely because she already has a spouse. An unrecorded Isobel remains possible and the candidate list is not exhaustive. No mother is named in the 1612 baptism review, so none is selected for the bride. David’s own selected Andrew-of-Calder father remains uncertain and supplies no independent corroboration. Existing relatives, dates and all confidently marked links are preserved. No identity merge, new original inspection, live WikiTree edit or confidence upgrade is claimed. Working connectivity counts the retained profile accounts, including possible duplicates.

chapters.title: Campbeltown: a provisional Linlithgow origin and Agnes’s placement
body: Select John Glasgow-1561 as the uncertain working father of George Glasgow-3100 of Campbeltown through possible identity with John’s indexed Linlithgow son George-1560 of 20 January 1622. A child baptised in 1622 could have been about 37 at Alexander’s 1659 Campbeltown event and about 28 in the approximate 1650 generation assigned to James and Agnes. This is a workable adult generation for the household. Prefer this comparison provisionally over the older 1605 Mid Calder George-1082, who would have been about 54 in 1659, without excluding that man. The 1627 Glasgow George-1090 is a close alternative, about 32 in 1659; his profile also carries a separate, unproved Fanne Smith household association requiring its own identity review. The preference is weak and practical: the 1622 child has no established incompatible adult fate, and the household timing is compatible. Missing later records are not positive identity evidence. No shared occupation, holding, spouse, witness or migration record identifies the Linlithgow child with the Campbeltown father. This is a very low-confidence family selection, not an identified migration or a record naming the adult’s father.

Select George Glasgow-3100 as Agnes Glasgow-1562’s uncertain working father. This activates the existing geographic family suggestion: Agnes’s captured profile places her Longwill household in Campbeltown, with a 1670 marriage-year field and a son’s 1683 birth field, while George is the named father in the 1659 Campbeltown event. Their approximate parent/child generations permit an older daughter in that household. The same locality and generation make daughter a useful provisional placement alongside George’s attached James and recorded Alexander. The marriage year, child details and Agnes’s circa-1650 birth are profile-held leads, not a newly inspected parish entry. No source names Agnes’s father; a sister, cousin, other local family or unrecorded father remains possible.

George-1560 and George-3100 remain separate profile accounts of a possible single man; shared proposed parentage does not prove two distinct sons called George or an identity merge. The 1605 and 1627 childhood candidates remain viable, and the list is not exhaustive. A separate unrecorded childhood is possible. The illustrative ages assume baptism near birth. George-3100’s 1630 structured and 1640 narrative births are unsupported estimates; neither is silently replaced by a proved 1622 birth. The existing John review cites X1RN-XV7 whereas the child profile cites X1RN-XVQ; retain that reference difference for original-register comparison, without treating the citations as independent events. James-1496’s father link to George is inherited and unproved; its name pattern supplies no independent corroboration for the chosen childhood. Agnes’s 1670 marriage field does not establish her age. No birth year is altered to force a generation. Assess mothers separately. No mother is supplied for the 1622 child in this review and none is selected for the Campbeltown adult. Grizel Dunlop-3562 is already the confidently marked mother of Alexander-3101 in the 1659 event, but that does not establish her maternity of Agnes or James. Her circa-1640 birth is also an unsupported estimate. Neither James nor Agnes receives a mother. The FMP 13 April 1659 birth-date field and Scotland’s People 12 April index date remain literal alternatives; the original entry and reference conventions are unresolved. The Auchinhork residence reading is not assigned a guessed modern place. John-1561’s own Andrew-of-Calder father and his other childhood-to-adult comparisons remain uncertain. No new original inspection, confident relationship upgrade, live WikiTree edit or identity merge is claimed. Connectivity counts profile accounts and retains the possible duplicate.

chapters.title: Three more early family placements, explicitly uncertain
body: The local working tree now selects William of Saltmarket as Michael of Stevenston’s possible father, Andrew of Calder as Jonat Menzeis’s possible father, and Ninian as Barbara Wilson’s possible father. These choices use the existing brother/cousin, same-parish remarriage and daughter/niece comparisons.

Michael Glasgow of Stevenston: The existing Stevenston study places Michael as a probable brother or cousin of James elder of Corsankell, rather than his son. Michael was an adult witness in the Glencairn estate network in 1549; both appear in the same small estate landscape in the 1559–60 teind list. Their approximate 1525 and 1515 generations fit brothers. Select the brother option provisionally and extend James’s already uncertain father William to Michael. This uses an existing older household without inventing an intervening person. The Mathie–Glencairn network supplies a credible route between the burgh family and these estates. Limits: The brother-versus-cousin choice is unresolved, and James’s own father William is uncertain. No record calls Michael William’s son. A cousin through another burgh household, an older generation than the estimated 1525 birth, or a separate family remains possible. Brakpleuch and Dubbs may represent one Michael or two. No mother, exact birth or death is inferred.

Jonat Glasgow, wife of David Menzeis: Jonat is the mother in a Mid Calder baptism in 1609. The existing comparison prefers her possible identity with Jonet Glasgow who married Martin Ramsy in the same parish in 1624, fifteen years later. That Jonet is already placed as Andrew’s testament daughter. Select Andrew as Jonat’s uncertain father through this local identity reconstruction. Her estimated 1585 generation fits Andrew’s household; the same name, parish and feasible remarriage sequence favour this model over the more distant Ninian household. Limits: This combines two uncertain identity steps: the 1609 mother with the 1624 bride, and the bride with Andrew’s testament daughter. David Menzeis’s death and the bride’s widowhood are not recorded in the material reviewed. Jonat and Jonet may be different women; retain both profiles and do not count an identity merge. Ninian Glasgow remains a competing father hypothesis. No mother is attached.

Barbara Glasgow, wife of Johne Wilsoune: The existing branch assessment already favours Barbara as a daughter or niece of Ninian. Her 1611 South Leith marriage entry fits the Leith setting of Ninian’s possible son William and the adjoining Edinburgh craft households; Ninian’s documented son Robert was a cordiner. The estimated 1590 daughter generation fits Ninian’s estimated 1550 generation. Select daughter as the simpler working placement within this already identified household, while retaining niece as an alternative. This is a combined locality, generation and family-network inference. Limits: Neither the marriage entry nor Ninian’s testament names Barbara as his daughter. The proposed Leith brother William is himself uncertain, and shared craft geography is suggestive rather than individual proof. Barbara may instead be Ninian’s niece or belong to another local family. If she is Barbara-567, the existing William-3522 father claim becomes a rival explanation. The adult Barbara identities remain separate, the 1611 date discrepancy stays open, and no mother is assigned.

Each is low confidence and counts only as a selected uncertain parent in the working graph. Keep possible duplicate profiles separate, mothers independent, and the confident graph unchanged. No new source reading is claimed.

chapters.title: Four selected working connections
body: The local working tree now selects Andrew of Calder as tentative father of James, John of Linlithgow and David of Mid Calder. It selects the older Mid Calder/Quothquan John as tentative father of the1640s Kirknewton John. These are logical reconstructions from material already on this site, not newly discovered parentage records.

James Glasgow → Andrew Glasgow of Calder: Andrew’s documented rural Calder household is the preferred working anchor for James’s nearby Mid Calder family. He was alive across the estimated1575–1586 birth interval of all three Lothian fathers; Hermand John’s1577 death would require an earlier birth estimate for David. That favours this coherent provisional family without excluding the other father. Andrew was alive until1598 and the uncertain generations allow James to be an older son. This uses the actual Calder setting and compatible family sequence, not the withdrawn assertion that the testament named James. James’s Inveresk/Fisherrow identity remains a separate uncertainty. Alternatives: John of Hermand-3181 is another plausible older local father. The George named at Mureistoun1586 and the George witness1605 are a competing father/relative lead; identifying that George with merchant1099 would require additional identity assumptions and young fatherhood. None is excluded. Andrew’s omission of James weakens this model; it does not disprove an older son.

John Glasgow of Linlithgow → Andrew Glasgow of Calder: Select the same older Calder household as the working origin for this neighbouring Lothian family. John’s estimated1579 generation and children recorded1613–1622 fit an older son of Andrew, whose own father is tentatively John-1093. The proximity and compatible generations make this a useful shared-family model alongside James and David, rather than an assertion that the three are proved brothers. Alternatives: John of Hermand-3181 is a compatible alternative if John1561’s estimated birth is earlier than1577. A separate unnamed local father remains possible. Andrew’s1598 testament does not name John; do not restore the obsolete James/Andrew/William child list or attach Jonet Anderson as mother.

David Glasgow of Mid Calder → Andrew Glasgow of Calder: David’s1606 and1612 Mid Calder baptisms place his household in the same small Calder area as the earlier Andrew household. His approximate generation permits Andrew to be his father. The first recorded daughter Elspeth is consistent with the Elizat name in Andrew’s household, a minor naming clue rather than a mother identification. Select Andrew as the tentative shared father with James and John; exact birth years remain estimates. Alternatives: John of Hermand-3181 or another older local Glasgow could be the father. If David’s approximate1586 birth were established, he would have been young when omitted from Andrew’s1598 testament, making that omission more troublesome. It is not an established birth date. Elizat Stevinsoun and the discredited Jonet Anderson attribution are not automatically assigned as mothers.

John Glasgow of Kirknewton → John Glasgow, Mid Calder/Quothquan working identity: The older John already represents the father named in Mid Calder baptisms1608–1609. His son John-1086, baptised1608, is a viable earlier identity for the adult John who had children in neighbouring Kirknewton/East Calder1646–1650: age38 at the1646 birth is straightforward. Select the older John as working father of3610 on that local and chronological reconstruction. Keep the two son profiles separate while testing their possible identity. Alternatives: John-1086 has a later Biggar account that has not been equated with3610. They may be different men, and the older father’s Mid Calder/Montfoid/Quothquan identity is itself uncertain. Robert-4006 is another generationally compatible Calder father. This does not restore the former unsupported William-1087 father or treat1629 as a recorded birthday.
All four edges are uncertain and count only in the working pedigree. Confident relationships, raw WikiTree parent fields and the fixed cohort are unchanged. No mother is assigned by these selections.

chapters.title: Record limits behind the working parent selections
body: John Glasgow is the father named at Linlithgow baptisms in 1613, 1617 and 1622; David is named at Mid Calder baptisms in 1606 and 1612. Their live parent fields are empty, as checked 15 October 2026, while biography prose still repeats the superseded Andrew/Jonet testament rationale. Complete local amendments retain the sources and wider family hypotheses.

John’s proposed child Thomas, indexed in Glasgow in 1612, has recorded father George Glasgow and mother Margaret Steuart. This is a conflict for the record-defined child; later adult Thomas identities remain a separate question.

The former John-3608 now resolves to John-3296. His associated Mid Calder 1608/1609 father entries and the Linlithgow sequence are compatible, but no shared wife, occupation, holding or cross-parish identity is established. Original parish pages and named heirs are the next connection test. No paternal join or certainty upgrade is counted.
These limits remain in force. The local working model now selects Andrew3163 as uncertain father of John and David, rather than leaving the compatible branches unplaced; no parent is newly proved.

body: The document does not name Jonet Anderson as wife, nor James, Andrew or William as children; those former readings cannot support a pedigree.
The rural household's succession plan is direct evidence within the family, not a bridge to the Glasgow burgh or Hirmenschelis Johns.
